analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling or transferring people's location and health data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was introduced in the final two weeks of the 118th Congress and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that buy and resell information about individuals — to sell, share, or transfer data showing where a person has been or what their health status is, including pregnancy, miscarriage, mental health, disability, and searches for health services. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the ban, and violators could face fines of up to 15% of their parent company's annual revenue. The bill was introduced on December 19, 2024, with only two weeks left in the session, and was referred to committee without any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose movements or health information is bought and resold without their knowledge. The bill defines health data to include pregnancy, miscarriage, disability, mental health conditions, and even searches for health care, so it would cover the app and location data that data brokers currently package and sell. People in states where reproductive health care is restricted would have less of that information available for resale.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose location and health data is resold

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from selling, licensing, trading, or otherwise making available location data and health data, whether directly collected or inferred from other information [S2].
Defines health data broadly to include pregnancy, miscarriage, disability, physical and mental health conditions, and attempts to obtain health services [S2].

Gives the FTC, state attorneys general, and private individuals the power to sue violators, seek deletion of improperly transferred data, and obtain civil penalties of up to 15% of a violator's ultimate parent entity's prior-year revenues [S2].

Carves out HIPAA-compliant handling by covered entities and business associates, publication of newsworthy information, and disclosures the individual explicitly authorizes, so the ban targets the resale market rather than ordinary health care or journalism [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the app and advertising companies that feed them location and health data would lose a resale market, and some ad-supported free apps that monetize location data would lose that revenue stream.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $1 billion to the FTC to carry out the law, a large new spending commitment for one agency's enforcement effort [S2].

The definition of 'data broker' — a person that collects, buys, licenses, or infers data and then sells, licenses, or trades it — and the FTC's rulemaking to define 'data' would leave the boundary of the ban to regulatory interpretation, creating compliance uncertainty for firms that touch location or health information [S2].

Routing enforcement through the FTC and exclusive jurisdiction in federal courts concentrates enforcement in one agency, and a future administration could choose to enforce it loosely; private suits require the plaintiff to show their own interest was affected [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — keeping records of where people go and their health status, including pregnancy and miscarriage, out of a resale market — is substantial at a time when such data can be bought by anyone, and the exceptions for HIPAA-covered handling, journalism, and authorized disclosures limit the burden on health care and the press. The main honest costs are the $1 billion appropriation and compliance uncertainty for firms near the edge of the 'data broker' definition.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with two weeks left in the session and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on December 19, 2024, in the final two weeks of the 118th Congress [S1].

The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no report, no floor action — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
The bill attracted three cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the location-data advertising ecosystem keep selling health and location information, since no restriction took effect.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill received no committee action in the Republican-controlled House before the session ended [S2][S3][S4].

industries.note: Their core business is collecting and reselling information about individuals; the bill makes it unlawful to sell or transfer location and health data, with civil penalties up to 15% of parent-entity revenue [S2].
Apps and ad networks that monetize users' movements by feeding location data to brokers would lose that revenue channel, since transfers of location data would be prohibited [S2].

industries.industry: Health and wellness app makers and period trackers
industries.note: The bill covers health data collected by non-HIPAA apps, including pregnancy and miscarriage information, blocking resale of that data; if they sell or license user data they lose that stream, while apps that do not sell data are largely unaffected [S2].
